title: Your first website, built by AI
promise: You're going to have your website with your real text and your real prices. You'll see it open in your phone's browser, at an internet address you can send over WhatsApp. And all without writing a line of code or opening the terminal.
why: Lucía Bermejo makes custom cakes in Getafe and has 3,200 Instagram followers. She was answering the same private message forty times a day: how much does a two-tier cake cost. She'd been quoted €1,400 for a website and had let it slide for two years. Every time she tried, she ended up on a tutorial that started with installing things. One Tuesday afternoon she sat down with Claude, wrote a long message with her real prices, and twenty-five minutes later she had a file that opened on her phone. The next day she published it at a free address and put it in her Instagram bio link.

theory.title: A website is a text file. That's it
theory.text: A web page isn't a mysterious program: it's a text file with markup inside it. The language of that markup is called HTML (the language web pages are written in). You can open the file with Windows Notepad and read it, even if you don't understand half of it. The browser (the program you use to get on the internet: Chrome, Safari, Edge) reads that text and paints it. Where it finds a heading marker it draws a big heading; where it finds a button marker, it draws a button. Here's the trick behind this whole lesson: writing text is exactly the one thing an AI is best at. That's why a simple website is one of the things it does best. The doubt that comes up now is obvious: if it's this easy, why does someone charge €1,400 for a website? Because the expensive part isn't the file, it's everything around it: deciding what to put on it, the photos, keeping it alive, hooking it up to payments and bookings, and answering the day it breaks. The file for your first version, you have today in twenty-five minutes and it doesn't cost you a cent.
theory.analogy: It's like sheet music. The paper with the notes doesn't make a sound; it sounds when someone plays it. Your HTML file is the sheet music and the browser is the pianist: any browser in the world reads the same sheet music and plays the same thing.
theory.example: Lucía's website ended up being a file called index.html, 380 lines and 21 KB, less than a phone photo. Inside were her three cakes with their prices (€35, €60, and from €95), her WhatsApp, her hours, and her two colors.

theory.title: One single file, and the terminal is off-limits
theory.text: If you just ask for a website with no further instructions, the AI will do what a professional would: give you three separate files, one for the text, one for the colors, and one for the behavior. Quite often it'll also suggest React or Next.js (tools for building large websites). Those tools require installing programs and typing commands in the terminal (that black screen where you type commands). For your first website, that's a wall people get stuck at. You need to ask for exactly the opposite, and ask for it in writing: a single file with everything inside, that opens by double-clicking. The advantages are very practical: you can email it, open it with the wifi off, save it on your desktop, and when something breaks, there's only one place to look. The reasonable doubt is whether this is amateur stuff. It isn't: serious companies have sales pages that are a single loose file, precisely because they load fast and don't break. The day you truly need several files, once you have three or four different pages, you ask for it and it splits it up for you in one message. Starting small doesn't close any doors for you; starting big does close the afternoon on you.

theory.title: The prompt decides everything, and half of it is stuff only you know
theory.text: AI is better at writing HTML than most people. What it doesn't know is what you charge, what your business is called, what your customers always ask, or what things you're embarrassed to put on there. It fills every gap you leave with the internet's average, and it fills it well: believable prices, a review from some Mary G. who doesn't exist, nine-to-eight hours that aren't yours. A prompt (the message you send it all at once) that works has six blocks: what it is and for whom, the single action you want whoever visits to take, your exact details, what you do NOT want, how it has to hand it over, and how you're going to check it. The block almost everyone skips is the fourth. It's the one that stops a shopping cart from showing up on the site of someone who doesn't sell anything online. There's one sentence inside the prompt worth its weight in gold: if you're missing a piece of data, write MISSING DATA and ask me, don't make it up. With that sentence, instead of a fake phone number you get a question.
theory.example: Lucía wrote out her three priced cakes (birthday €35, two-tier €60, wedding from €95), her WhatsApp, her real order policy of five days' notice, and a line that said: I don't make gluten-free cakes, make that clear. That NOT line saved her the question she got most every week.

theory.title: The whole file, no shortcuts: the rule that saves your afternoon
theory.text: The bug that makes most people give up doesn't happen while building, it happens while delivering. You ask for a change and it gives you back only the changed piece, or the whole file but with a "...(rest stays the same)..." in the middle. Since you don't know how to code, you can't stitch that piece back into place, and that's where the project ends. The rule has to be repeated in every message, with these words: give me back the entire file, first line to last, no shortcuts and no ellipses. There's a spot where this happens almost automatically: the side panel, called Artifact in Claude and Canvas in ChatGPT and Gemini. It's a window that opens to the right of the conversation with your file inside, with a copy button and a download button. In Claude, it also shows you the page already rendered as it's being written. If your app doesn't open it on its own, just ask: put it in the side panel. And if it tells you it's too long, the right answer is send it to me in two messages in a row, but whole: splitting the file is acceptable, summarizing it never is.

theory.title: One change at a time, and numbered copies on the desktop
theory.text: When you see the first version, seven things will pop into your head all at once: the blue, the title, the order of the prices, the button, the missing photo. If you send them all in one message, it rewrites the whole file and gives you back a version where three things are better and two things that used to work are now broken. There'll be no way to know which one broke which. The discipline is: one change per message, look at it, save it, ask for the next one. And keep numbered copies on your desktop, web-1.html, web-2.html, web-3.html. There's no undo button in a chat, and going back to the version from twenty minutes ago is impossible if you overwrote it. It costs ten seconds per copy, and the day something breaks you'll open the previous one and keep going from there instead of starting from zero. The typical worry is whether your desktop will fill up with files: you'll have six or seven, then delete the middle ones, and it works out much cheaper than losing an afternoon.
theory.analogy: It's like painting a wall and taking a photo after each coat. If the fourth coat comes out terrible, you know exactly which photo to go back to instead of arguing from memory about which color was the right one.

theory.title: From your desktop to an internet address, without touching the terminal
theory.text: A file on your desktop can't be opened by your client on the bus. For that it has to sit on a computer that's always on, and that's called hosting. The way with no terminal and no card is dragging a folder: go to app.netlify.com/drop, drop a folder containing your file named index.html into it. In about twenty seconds you get an address like happy-cake-1a2b3c.netlify.app, which works on any phone in the world. It's free on its starter plan. It'll ask you to create a free account only if you want to keep it and be able to update it later. Serious, hard-to-undo warning: publishing means making it public. Anyone can read what you upload, and search engines and automated programs copy it. So think twice before putting your personal phone number, your home address, or a client's name on it. Taking something down off the internet isn't instant and can take weeks to disappear from Google. The nice name, that tartasdelucia.com, is the only thing that costs money: about €12 a year, and it gets added later without rebuilding anything. And if you want people to write to you from the site, don't add a form yet: a loose file doesn't send emails no matter how much it looks like it does. A WhatsApp link and an email link, on the other hand, work from minute one and are free.

tasks.title: Write your data sheet before opening the AI
tasks.where: In Windows Notepad, in your phone's Notes app, or on paper. Still outside the AI.
tasks.action: Almost everything that's going to go wrong goes wrong here, so give it five real minutes. Write these nine lines with your real details, not approximate ones: 1) the exact name, spelled the way you want it read; 2) what you do, in one sentence; 3) your city; 4) three things you sell or do, each with its price in dollars; 5) your phone or WhatsApp with all the digits; 6) your email; 7) your hours or your real policy, like orders with five days' notice; 8) a sentence you want the page to open with; 9) the ONE thing you want whoever visits to do: message you on WhatsApp, call you, email you, or sign up for something. If you're missing any of that data, write MISSING DATA in its place. Don't leave it blank, because a blank spot is an invitation for it to be made up. Save the file as notes.txt on your desktop, because you'll paste it into the prompt in two minutes.
tasks.expect: A notes.txt file with nine lines, three prices in dollars, and a phone number with all its digits. If reading it back you can't say what the single action from point 9 is, it's not finished yet.
tasks.stuck: If you get stuck on point 9 because you want people to do three things, pick the one that would make you money tomorrow and shelve the other two. If you get stuck on the prices because they depend on the case, write the cheapest price with the word starting in front: starting at $95. It's honest information and it saves you forty messages of people asking.

tasks.title: Open a new chat and locate the side panel
tasks.where: At claude.ai, chatgpt.com, or gemini.google.com, from your computer's browser. Better on a computer than a phone today.
tasks.action: Open the app and press the new conversation button: in Claude it's the pencil-and-paper icon, top left; in ChatGPT it says New chat in the same spot; in Gemini it says New chat. Starting clean matters a lot here: if you're still in an old conversation, you drag along things you said days ago and you'll end up with a website contaminated by another project. Before typing anything, look at the dropdown at the top, where the model's name shows up, and choose the most capable one your plan allows. The app usually labels it as the most advanced or the one that reasons. It's worth using the good one here, because writing 400 coherent lines in one go is exactly where the difference shows. If you're on Claude you'll have one thing going for you: when it writes a web page, a window will open on its own to the right called Artifact. You'll see the page rendered as it's being built. In ChatGPT and Gemini that window is called Canvas and sometimes it only shows you the file's text, not rendered. That's fine: you'll see it the same way once you save it in the next step.
tasks.expect: An empty conversation, with the text box at the bottom and the model name at the top. No earlier messages above it.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the model selector, stop looking and go with whatever comes by default. The prompt in the next task is detailed enough to work with any of the three. If you only have your phone that works too, but copying the file will be more awkward: in that case use Claude and its panel's download button.

tasks.title: Paste the master prompt and answer its three questions
tasks.where: In the text box of the new conversation.
tasks.action: Copy the whole prompt below and, before sending it, replace everything between brackets with what's in notes.txt. Don't delete any block even if it seems repetitive: each one is covering a specific mistake that always happens. Notice the prompt ends by forbidding it from building right away and asking it to first summarize what it understood and ask you at most three questions. Answer them in a single message, short and with concrete details, and only then will it write the file. That ninety-second detour is what separates a website with your real prices from one with made-up prices.
tasks.prompt:
I want you to build me a simple website and I want to be able to open it today. I don't know how to code, I'm not going to use the terminal, and I'm not going to install anything. All the work happens inside this conversation.

WHAT IT IS AND WHO IT'S FOR
- Name, exactly as it should read: [NAME]
- What I do, in one sentence: [SENTENCE]
- City: [CITY]
- Who visits the page: [WHO, APPROXIMATE AGE, WHAT THEY'RE LOOKING FOR]. Eight out of ten arrive on mobile and in a hurry.

THE ONE ACTION
When someone finishes reading, I want them to do ONE thing: [MESSAGE ME ON WHATSAPP / CALL ME / EMAIL ME / SIGN UP]. Anything that doesn't push toward that is extra.

MY REAL DETAILS (use them exactly as given, don't change a single figure)
- Phone / WhatsApp: [NUMBER]
- Email: [EMAIL]
- What I do, with exact prices:
  1. [SERVICE 1] — $[PRICE]
  2. [SERVICE 2] — $[PRICE]
  3. [SERVICE 3] — $[PRICE]
- Hours or real policy: [HOURS OR TIMEFRAME]
- Sentence I want the page to open with: [SENTENCE]

If you're missing any piece of data, do NOT make it up: write MISSING DATA in its place and ask me. I'd rather have a marked gap than a nice-looking fake fact.

WHAT I DON'T WANT
No cart, no payments. No blog, no news section. No sign-up, no passwords. No embedded map. No filler Latin text. No review, testimonial, award, logo, customer count, or guarantee I haven't written for you. No photo that doesn't exist.

HOW YOU HAVE TO DELIVER IT (this is the most important part of all)
1. A SINGLE complete HTML file, from the first line to the last.
2. Everything inside that same file: colors and sizes inside a style tag, and any behavior inside a script tag. No separate files.
3. It has to work with no internet: don't link fonts, libraries, or outside images. With the wifi off it has to look exactly the same. If you need an icon, draw it inside the file or use an emoji.
4. No React, Next.js, Tailwind, npm, node, or any step that makes me open the terminal.
5. Put it in the side panel (Artifact or Canvas). If you can't, in a single code block with a copy button.
6. Writing "...same as before...", "continues as it was" or any shortcut is forbidden. If it comes out too long, tell me and send it in two messages in a row, but whole.

HOW IT SHOULD LOOK
- Mobile first: a single column, at least 16-pixel text, buttons at least 48 pixels tall so they can be tapped with a thumb.
- Colors: [TWO COLORS YOU LIKE, OR WRITE: pick something sober yourself and tell me which ones you used].
- Order from top to bottom: name and opening sentence, what I do, prices, big contact button, footer with phone and email.
- Also decent-looking on a computer, without overcomplicating it.

HOW I'M GOING TO CHECK IT (build it with this list in mind)
1. I save the file, double-click it, and it opens in the browser with no errors.
2. In a narrow window I can read everything without zooming and without scrolling sideways.
3. My exact three prices and my exact phone number show up, and no data I didn't give you.
4. I press the big contact button and it takes me to WhatsApp with a message already written.
5. With the wifi off, the page still looks the same.
6. I search the page for the words Lorem, example, yourcompany, and 123456789, and none of them show up.

BEFORE WRITING ANYTHING
Summarize in five lines what you've understood and ask me at most THREE questions about what's missing. Wait for my answer. Then build it.
tasks.expect: First a short summary and at most three questions, no code at all. After you answer them, the file shows up in the panel on the right; in Claude, you'll also see the page rendered with your name and your prices.
tasks.stuck: If it starts writing code right away without asking anything, stop it: "You skipped the last instruction. Summarize in five lines what you understood and ask me your three questions before building." If it gives you back several separate files, reply: "Combine it all into a single HTML file with the styles inside style and the code inside script, and give it to me whole."

tasks.title: Save the file to your desktop and open it with a double-click
tasks.where: On your computer, outside the AI.
tasks.action: If the side panel has a download button, use it and skip half this task: save the file to the desktop and rename it web-1.html. If it only has a copy button, do it by hand. On Windows: click Copy in the panel, open Notepad (press Start and type Notepad), paste with Control and V, go to File and then Save as. In the Type dropdown pick All files, in Encoding pick UTF-8, type the name web-1.html and save it to the Desktop. That Type dropdown step is the one everyone skips. If you don't change it, the file saves as web-1.html.txt and opening it shows text instead of a page. On Mac: open TextEdit, go to Format and click Make Plain Text BEFORE pasting anything, paste, save as web-1.html, and uncheck the box that adds the .txt extension. Once you have it, double-click the file: your browser opens and there's your page.
tasks.expect: Your browser open with your name at the top, your three prices, and your contact button. In the address bar you'll see something starting with file:/// and ending in web-1.html, and that's correct: you're opening it from your disk, not from the internet.
tasks.stuck: If double-clicking shows you a bunch of letters and symbols instead of the page, the file is called web-1.html.txt. On Windows open File Explorer, go to View, and turn on File name extensions. Then you'll see the extra .txt and can remove it from the name. If accented letters show up as odd symbols, you saved it with the wrong encoding: go back to Save as and pick UTF-8.

tasks.title: Narrow the window and run the six checks yourself
tasks.where: With the page open in your computer's browser.
tasks.action: Don't ask the AI if it looks good, because it hasn't opened your screen: it's only rereading what it wrote. Grab the browser window's right edge with your mouse and drag it left until the window is about phone-width, roughly a hand's span. Now go through the list of six, one by one, and mark OK or NO next to each number: 1) everything reads without zooming; 2) there's no bar at the bottom to scroll sideways; 3) your three prices are exactly yours; 4) the phone number is yours, digit by digit; 5) press Control and F, search for the words Lorem, example, yourcompany, and 123456789, and check none of them show up; 6) turn off wifi, reload with F5, and check it looks the same. The sixth is the one that gives the most surprises. It often sneaks in a font downloaded from outside, and without a connection the page's whole look changes.
tasks.expect: Six notes, with at least four OKs. The NOs are normal on the first version and are exactly what you're going to ask to fix in the next task, one at a time.
tasks.stuck: If the page overflows sideways in the narrow window, note exactly which element overflows (the price table, a long headline, an image) because you'll need to tell it. If the font changes with the wifi off, write: "You're loading an outside font. Remove it and use only system fonts, so it looks the same offline."

tasks.title: Ask for one single change and save the numbered copy
tasks.where: In the same conversation, with the page open next to it.
tasks.action: Take the first NO from your list and only that one. Send the prompt below with a single change in it. When it gives you back the file, save it as web-2.html, next to web-1.html and never over it. Open it and run through your whole list of six again, not just the point you fixed. Repeat the cycle for each NO, bumping the number: web-3.html, web-4.html. It looks slow and it's the exact opposite: whoever asks for seven changes at once ends up taking three times as long because they don't know what broke what.
tasks.prompt:
Change number [N]. Only this and nothing else:

[DESCRIBE THE CHANGE IN ONE SENTENCE. If it's text, write the exact text you want it to say. If it's something overflowing the screen, say exactly which element it is.]

Rules for this change:
1. Don't touch anything else in the file: not colors, not text, not order, not sizes I didn't ask for.
2. Give me back the WHOLE file again, first line to last, no shortcuts and no "...same as before...".
3. Below the file, write me two lines: what exactly you changed and where on the page I see it when I open it.
4. If making this change requires touching something that already worked, STOP and tell me before doing it, instead of patching it on your own.
5. Still no internet: no outside fonts, images, or libraries.
tasks.expect: The whole file again in the panel, plus two lines explaining what it touched and where to look. Opening web-2.html, that point becomes OK and the other five stay as they were.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you back only a piece, reply with a single sentence: "Give me the complete file, first line to last, no shortcuts." If fixing one point breaks another that was already fine, write: "Fixing point 3 broke point 5, which used to work. Go back to the previous file and fix point 3 without touching the part for point 5." And if that happens twice in a row, open web-1.html, start from there, and ask for smaller changes.

tasks.title: Make WhatsApp, email, and the phone actually work
tasks.action: This is where your page stops being a flyer and starts bringing in clients. Send the prompt below with your number written with no spaces, no dashes, and no plus sign: if your phone is 555 123 4567, you write 15551234567. Pay attention to point 4 of the prompt, because it's the one that saves you a headache: a form with checkboxes inside a loose file doesn't send anything anywhere. If you add one, your clients will type their order, press Send, and it'll never reach you. A WhatsApp button that works today beats a pretty form that lies.
tasks.prompt:
Now I want the contact to actually work, without signing up for any service and without me installing anything.

1. WHATSAPP BUTTON: add a link to https://wa.me/1[MY NUMBER WITH NO SPACES, NO DASHES, NO PLUS SIGN] with a message already written that says exactly: "[MESSAGE TEXT, FOR EXAMPLE: Hi, I saw your website and wanted to ask about...]". Make it the biggest, most visible button on the page.
2. EMAIL BUTTON: add a mailto link to [MY EMAIL], with the subject already filled in: "[SUBJECT]".
3. FOOTER PHONE: make the number in the footer tappable so that touching it on a phone dials it directly.
4. NO FORMS with checkboxes and a submit button. I know a loose file doesn't send emails and I don't want a button that tricks my clients into thinking their message got to me.
5. Tell me in one plain-language line what I should search for inside the file the day I want to change the phone number or the email myself.
6. Below that, explain in three lines what it would take the day I do want a form that actually reaches me: what service you'd use, what I'd have to do, and how much it costs a month in dollars.

Give me back the whole file, first line to last, no shortcuts.
tasks.expect: The complete file, a big WhatsApp button, and below it the line telling you what to search for to change the number plus the three lines about the form. Save this version and open it: pressing the button from the computer will open WhatsApp Web with the message already written.
tasks.stuck: If pressing the button takes you to WhatsApp but it says the number doesn't exist, it's almost always the format: check it and remove spaces, dashes, parentheses, and the plus sign, leaving only your country code followed by your digits with no separators. If it snuck a form in anyway, write: "Remove the whole form. I don't want a submit button that doesn't send anything."

tasks.title: Ask the AI to hunt down its own mistakes
tasks.where: In the same conversation, with the version you already like.
tasks.action: Before showing it to anyone, turn it against its own work. This prompt is mostly for catching what it made up itself and you haven't spotted: a fake review, an award, a satisfied-customer figure, hours that aren't yours. Read through its whole list and decide yourself what gets fixed and what doesn't. Don't tell it to fix everything at once, because you'd land right back in the same problem. Pick the three worst issues and ask for them one at a time with the single-change prompt from the previous task.
tasks.prompt:
Turn against your own work. Review the file you just gave me and find its flaws. Do NOT fix it yet: just make me the list.

Specifically look for:
1. MADE-UP DATA: any price, name, address, email, phone, hours, review, award, customer count, or guarantee I didn't write for you. Quote them to me one by one with the exact text you used.
2. FILLER TEXT: Lorem ipsum, "your text here", "example company", numbers like 123456789.
3. THINGS THAT NEED THE INTERNET: outside fonts, linked images, libraries. I want zero. Tell me how many there are.
4. PROBLEMS ON A 360-PIXEL-WIDE SCREEN: text that overflows, buttons under 48 pixels tall, text under 16 pixels, anything that forces sideways scrolling.
5. LINKS AND BUTTONS that go nowhere or do nothing when pressed.
6. PROMISES I DIDN'T WRITE: deadlines, guarantees, "the best in the city", "over 500 customers".

Give it back to me as a three-column table: WHAT I FOUND / WHY IT'S A PROBLEM FOR ME / HOW TO FIX IT. Order it from most serious to least serious.

If you can't verify something yourself from here, say so clearly instead of assuming it's fine.

Don't write the corrected file yet. Wait for me to tell you which ones we're fixing.
tasks.expect: A table with three to ten lines, sorted by severity. What's interesting is the first row under point 1: almost always some piece of data shows up that you never wrote, and it's been there since the first version.
tasks.stuck: If it tells you everything's perfect and finds nothing, push back: "It's very unlikely there isn't a single flaw. Give me at least five things that could be improved, even minor ones, and rank them by severity." If it gives you back the corrected file without you asking, ignore it and keep the list: you're going to ask for the changes one at a time.

tasks.title: Publish it by dragging a folder, with no terminal
tasks.where: On your desktop first, then at app.netlify.com/drop, in the browser.
tasks.action: Before anything, read this: publishing means making it public, and anyone can see and copy what you upload, including automated programs that scrape phone numbers and emails. If you're going to put your personal cell number on there, accept that going in. Once you've decided, create a new folder on the desktop called my-website, copy your good version inside it, and rename it exactly index.html, lowercase and nothing else after it. That name isn't arbitrary: it's the file that shows up when someone visits your address without asking for anything specific. Leave only that file inside the folder, without the numbered versions. Now open app.netlify.com/drop, drag the whole my-website folder from your desktop into the box asking you to drop your folder there, and wait about twenty seconds. You'll get an address like happy-cake-1a2b3c.netlify.app. It's free. It'll ask you to create a free account if you want to keep it and be able to update it later, and you create that account yourself, with your email.
tasks.expect: An address ending in .netlify.app that you can copy. Open it on your phone with mobile data and wifi off: there's your real website, on the internet, and that's the lesson's moment. Press the WhatsApp button from your phone and check that the conversation opens with the message already written.
tasks.stuck: If you get a page-not-found error, it's almost always the file name: it has to be exactly index.html, lowercase, not index.html.txt or Index.html. If you dragged the loose file instead of the folder, do it again with the whole folder. If it looks different on the phone than on the computer, reload by pulling the screen down: it's usually an old copy cached in the browser.

tasks.title: Save the kit so you don't start from zero tomorrow
tasks.where: In the same conversation, and then in a text file on your desktop.
tasks.action: Everything you've decided in this conversation disappears the moment you close it, and tomorrow you'll start with an AI that doesn't remember your name or your prices. Send the prompt below, copy what it gives back, and paste it into a new file called web-kit.txt on your desktop, next to your numbered versions. The second part, the cheat sheet, is the one you'll use most. It tells you what word to search for with Control and F inside the file to change a price yourself, without opening any conversation.
tasks.prompt:
Wrap up the job. Give me these three things in a single block of text I can copy and paste into a file:

1. THE STARTER PROMPT, updated with everything we've decided today and with my real details already written into it, so that the day I open a new conversation I can paste it and pick up here instead of from zero. Include the fixed rules: single file, nothing that needs the internet, no terminal, whole file with no shortcuts, and one change per message.

2. THE CHEAT SHEET FOR MY FILE: where I go to change each thing, one line per thing. The name, the opening sentence, each of the three prices, the WhatsApp number, the email, and the two colors. On each line, tell me the exact text I need to search for with Control and F to find it.

3. THE NEXT THREE STEPS, ranked from most to least useful, and for each one: what I gain, how much it costs a year in dollars, and how much time it takes me.

No introduction and no closing: just the text, so I can paste it as-is and use it a month from now.
tasks.expect: A block of text with three sections and no surrounding explanations. The cheat sheet has to give you specific text to search for, like search for $60 to change the two-tier cake's price, not vague pointers like search the pricing section.
tasks.stuck: If it gives it back full of comments and introductions, reply: "Give me only the kit's text, no introduction or closing, so I can copy it all at once." If the cheat sheet tells you things you can't search for, write: "On each cheat sheet line, write me the literal text that appears inside the file, so I can find it with Control and F."

matters: Putting your real details into the prompt, with exact figures. If you don't write them, it doesn't stay blank: it makes up believable prices, a review from someone who doesn't exist, and hours that aren't yours. It hurts because it all looks lovely, you accept it, publish it, and your first client calls asking for the price of something you don't sell.

Demanding the whole file, no shortcuts, in every message. A "...(rest stays the same)..." in the middle of the answer turns your project into a puzzle you can't assemble because you can't read code. Most people who give up on an AI-built website give up right here. And it wasn't their fault or the model's: it was an eleven-word sentence nobody told them to write.

One change per message and numbered copies on the desktop. If you ask for seven things at once, it rewrites the whole file and gives you back three improvements and two breakages, with no way to know which one caused which. And with no copies there's no going back: a conversation has no undo button. The good version from twenty minutes ago stops existing the moment you overwrite it.

Checking it yourself, with the narrow window, before showing it to anyone. When it tells you it looks perfect on mobile, it's describing what it wrote, not looking at a screen, because it can't open your file. Eight out of ten visits are going to come from a phone. A headline that overflows off the right side is the first thing your client sees and the last thing they do before closing it.
ignore: React, Next.js, Tailwind, npm, and anything that starts with installing. Those are excellent tools for sites with hundreds of pages and several people working at once. Your first website is a file, and dragging in those tools now only adds five more steps that can break.

Your own domain, that yourbusiness.com. It costs about $12 a year and can be plugged in later without rebuilding a single thing on the page. A free address ending in .netlify.app works perfectly for sending over WhatsApp and putting in your Instagram bio while you check whether the site is bringing you clients.

Showing up on Google. Appearing in search results is a separate job, taking months, and doesn't depend on how the file is built. Almost all your first visits are going to come because you sent the link, and for that the site is already ready from day one.
canDo: Write out 300 or 400 lines of a whole page in one go, with matching colors, readable text, and a layout that rearranges itself on mobile automatically. All in under two minutes and without getting the syntax wrong.
Give you back the complete file as many times as you ask, without getting tired, without complaining, and without charging more, as long as you ask for one change at a time.
Explain where each thing lives inside the file and the exact text to search for to change a price yourself, without opening another conversation.

Find its own fabrications if you ask explicitly: fake reviews, guarantees you never gave, hours that aren't yours. It doesn't do it on its own, but when you ask it pulls them out into an ordered list.
cantDo: It doesn't know your prices, your hours, your phone number, or how your customers talk. Anything you don't write for it, it fills in with the internet's average, and the result looks flawless and false, which is the most dangerous combination there is.

It can't open your file or see it on your phone. When it says "it looks perfect on small screens," it's describing what it just wrote, not looking at anything. That check is yours to make, by dragging the window's edge with your mouse.

It can't publish the website for you, create the hosting account, or buy the $12-a-year domain. Dragging the folder and creating the accounts are yours to do, and it's better that way: those are the keys to your website.

It doesn't make a form collect data by magic. A loose file doesn't send emails, so a submit button with no service behind it is deceptive. Your clients will think they've written to you when nothing actually arrived.
words: HTML
The language web pages are written in. It's plain text with markup around it that says this is a heading, this is a button, this is a photo.
Browser
The program you use to get on the internet: Chrome, Safari, Edge, or Firefox. It also opens a file saved on your computer, with no connection at all.
index.html
The name you have to give your main page's file. When someone types your address without asking for anything specific, this is the file that shows up.
Style tag
The part of the file where the colors, font sizes, spacing, and borders live. Changing things in there changes the whole page's look without touching a single word of the text.
Artifact or Canvas

The panel that opens to the right of the conversation with your file inside, separate from the messages. It comes with a button to copy the whole thing and another to download it, and sometimes shows you the page already rendered.
Hosting
Another company's computer, running twenty-four hours a day, where you leave your file so anyone can open it from home. Some sites do it for free for small pages.
Domain
The name people type to reach your page, for example tartasdelucia.com. It's not bought forever: it's rented by the year, around $12 a year.
Responsive
The page rearranging itself on its own depending on screen width: a single column on mobile, more spread out on a computer. It's not two different pages, it's the same one adapting.
Form

The block with fields to type into and a submit button. On its own it doesn't send anything anywhere: you need to separately sign up for a service that collects what people type and delivers it to you.
wa.me link and mailto link
Two ways of writing a link so that tapping it directly opens WhatsApp or email with the message already started. They cost nothing, need no sign-up anywhere, and work from minute one.
